analysis.one_liner: Exempts the first $5 million of an estate from the estate tax.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote; it died in the House Ways and Means Committee with 4 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the estate tax exemption so that the first $5 million of a person's estate passes to heirs tax-free, up from roughly $675,000 at the time. It would also repeal a separate, narrower deduction for family-owned businesses that Congress had created in 1997. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to estates worth between about $675,000 and $5 million — a group made up mostly of well-off families, owners of family businesses, and holders of farms or other substantial assets — would pay no estate tax on the first $5 million. Estate planning professionals would also keep a larger client base if exemptions were higher.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Heirs to estates up to $5 million

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets the estate and gift tax exclusion at $5 million, meaning estates and lifetime gifts up to that amount owe no federal tax.
By repealing section 2057 of the tax code, it eliminates the separate family-owned business interest deduction, replacing the narrower 1997-era benefit with the broader $5 million exemption.
The change would have applied to deaths and gifts occurring after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury — and by extension taxpayers generally — would bear the cost, since taxes on estates between roughly $675,000 and $5 million would no longer be collected. That revenue loss is concentrated among benefits flowing to higher-wealth families.

drawbacks.text: In 2001 the estate tax already exempted estates up to about $675,000 (rising to $1 million under prior law), so most ordinary families never paid it; raising the exclusion to $5 million would primarily cut taxes for substantial estates rather than for middle-income families.
The bill provides no offsetting revenue, so the full cost of the higher exemption would add to the federal deficit.
Repealing the family-owned business deduction removes a targeted break for smaller family firms in favor of a blanket exemption that also covers large investment estates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real for family businesses and farms that feared estate taxes forcing a sale, but the $5 million exemption is a blunt instrument: most of its value goes to heirs of already-wealthy estates, and the bill offers no way to pay for the lost revenue. A supporter would call it a middle path between full repeal and the existing tax; a critic would call it an unnecessary tax cut for the top few percent of estates.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent straight to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Representative Patsy Mink of Hawaii introduced the bill on February 27, 2001.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax bills.
Four Democratic colleagues cosponsored the bill.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the remainder of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the estate tax remained as it was (later gradually changed by separate 2001 legislation), so the estate tax continued to apply to large estates above the then-existing exemption. Wealthy estates gained nothing from this particular bill, while the federal government kept the revenue it would have foregone.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large estates kept paying; Treasury kept the revenue

for.name: Rep. Patsy Mink
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise the estate tax exclusion to $5 million and gave introductory remarks.

against.name: Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee, to which the bill was referred, never scheduled a hearing or markup and never reported the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats sponsored and cosponsored the bill, but no vote was ever taken, so the record shows no opposition votes to measure the partisan split.

industries.note: A $5 million estate tax exemption would have eliminated tax on estates far above what most families ever accumulate, with the revenue cost falling on the federal Treasury. In 2001 the estate tax affected only a small share of the largest estates.
These were the bill's stated beneficiaries: owners whose estates included a business or farm would owe no estate tax up to $5 million, easing fears of selling the enterprise to pay the tax.
A higher exemption shrinks the number of estates needing tax planning, but larger exemptions also create new planning demand for gifts and wealth transfers up to the $5 million line.
